AI Playbook for
Account Management

The Leo guide to where AI genuinely helps account management today: which tool to use, what good looks like, and how to stay client-safe.

Leo UK · Publicis Groupe · 2026

★

The golden rule

Right task → right tool → client-safe.

At Leo, that also means: use AI to free up the thinking time that makes the work better, the brief sharper, the cultural rationale clearer, the sell more confident. The operational work should occupy less of your day. The work that gets people talking should be the focus.

Purpose

Populist Creativity is about making work that gets people talking. Not work that interrupts people, but work that moves through culture because real people choose to engage with it.

The account team is where the client brief is shaped, where the cultural rationale for an idea is built and articulated to a client, and where the relationship is managed that makes bold, conversation-starting work possible in the first place. AI is most useful in that context when it helps you work faster on the operational stuff, so you spend more time on the thinking and the relationship.

This playbook is deliberately narrow, covering only what we think AI is genuinely good at and useful for you right now. It's also not perfect — we're learning how to get the best out of the tools as we go. If you see problems that need fixing or opportunities to improve this playbook then please share your feedback.

Where AI helps, and where it doesn't

AI is strong for drafting, summarising, structuring, stress-testing and researching. It is not for client judgement, relationship decisions, or anything that requires reading the room. A human always owns those calls.

The two-minute version

  • Use CoPilot for everyday work inside Microsoft 365: drafting, summarising, structuring, stress-testing and prepping. It's here now, for everyone.
  • Use MRCL where enabled for connected Groupe data, pre-built Skills and research. Full rollout won't land until 2027; treat it as "available where enabled."
  • For image and video reference in concept development, use Google's tools in MRCL: Nano Banana for image, VEO for video. Treat outputs as reference only, never final craft.
  • Never put client data into any tool until the account's legal position is confirmed (Section 5).
  • AI drafts. A person decides. Nothing client-facing goes out without a human check.

Core responsibilities & use cases

Where AI fits in your work

The use cases in this playbook hang off six accountability areas that hold true across every level of the account team. They start with personal organisation, because getting the inbox, diary and weekly plan under control creates the space for stronger client leadership, clearer communication and better commercial judgement.

1
Personal organisation
Inbox triage and weekly schedule planning
▾
Account management runs on a lot of incoming: emails, meetings, requests and updates that need sorting before you can do the actual work. This covers two things: triaging what genuinely needs your attention in the inbox, and turning your diary into a working plan for the week — so the prep gets done, the meetings land well, and the operational load doesn't crowd out the thinking.
A) Inbox triage
📌 CoPilot

CoPilot has access to your Outlook and Teams activity, so just point it in the right direction (i.e. folder, client or topic).

A fast, clear read on what actually needs you today — not a summary of everything, a decision on what matters. Less time in the inbox, more on the work.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are an organised account lead for Leo UK prioritising live work for [CLIENT / TOPIC]. Context: I need a fast read on what actually needs action today from my recent emails. Task: Summarise and triage the messages by urgency and ownership. Output: Structure it as:
1) Urgent: replies or actions needed today
2) Waiting on me: things I need to move forward
3) Waiting on others: things I'm chasing
4) FYI only: no action required
5) Risks or escalations that need a senior call
For each item include sender, topic, required action and suggested timing.

Guardrails: Do not draft replies where client sensitivity or judgement is needed — flag those for human review. Do not guess at intent or urgency where context is missing.
Guardrails: Do not draft replies where client sensitivity or judgement is needed — flag those for human review. Do not guess at intent or urgency where context is missing.
▶ Output: Prioritised inbox triage covering what needs action today, what's waiting and what can wait
B) Weekly schedule & prep plan
📌 CoPilot

Your calendar for the week; any known deadlines, deliverables or client commitments that sit outside the diary.

A realistic working plan for the week — not an optimistic one. Meetings mapped to the prep they need, deliverables given time to get done, and any conflicts or gaps surfaced before they become problems.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are an organised account lead for Leo UK planning your working week. Context: Here is my diary for the week: [PASTE CALENDAR]. I also have the following deadlines and deliverables outside the diary: [LIST]. Task: Turn this into a practical working schedule. Output: Structure it as:
1) Meeting-by-meeting prep needed — what to review, draft or confirm before each one
2) Deliverables due this week with suggested time to complete them
3) A suggested daily priority order for Monday to Friday that balances meetings, prep and focused work time
4) Conflicts, gaps or risks in the schedule — things that look unmanageable or under-resourced

Guardrails: Be realistic, not optimistic. Flag where the schedule is too heavy. Do not invent deadlines or meeting objectives — flag where context is missing.
Guardrails: Be realistic, not optimistic. Flag where the schedule is too heavy rather than making it work on paper. Do not invent deadlines or meeting objectives.
▶ Output: Practical weekly plan covering meeting prep, deliverable timings, a daily priority order and any schedule risks
2
Client leadership prep
Client meeting and engagement prep plus growth thinking and portfolio narrative
▾
This covers the moments where account leads need to walk into a client engagement fully prepared: clear on the wider business context, the client's likely point of view, the relationship dynamics, and what Leo needs to land. Use it to turn mixed inputs into a practical prep note that helps the team manage the conversation with the right context in mind.
A) Client meeting & engagement prep
📌 CoPilot

Recent client emails, meeting notes, previous contact reports and relevant decks; meeting objective or agenda; attendee list and stakeholder context; known client priorities, sensitivities, business pressures, scope and commercial context.

A practical prep note that means you walk in ready: clear on the client's business context, what has changed, what the client is likely to care about, the point of view Leo should hold, likely questions, and the messages or decisions we need to land. It should help the team manage the engagement with relevant context in mind, not just summarise the inputs.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are a senior account lead for Leo UK preparing the team for an upcoming [MEETING / PITCH / REVIEW / CLIENT ENGAGEMENT] with [CLIENT]. Context: The engagement is about [TOPIC], and we need to walk in with a clear understanding of the wider business context, the client's likely point of view, the current relationship dynamics and what Leo needs to land. Use the supplied emails, meeting notes, previous contact reports, decks and stakeholder context only. Task: Create a practical prep note that turns the mixed inputs into a clear view of the client situation and the best way to manage the engagement. Output: Structure it as 1) Meeting objective, 2) Client situation now, 3) What has changed since we last engaged, 4) Client POV: what they are likely to care about, question or challenge, 5) Stakeholders in the room and relevant context for each, 6) Leo POV and recommended position, 7) Likely questions and suggested responses, 8) Our three key messages, 9) What we need from the client by the end, 10) Open risks, gaps or sensitivities to handle carefully.

Guardrails: Use only the supplied inputs. Flag missing context rather than filling it in. Do not invent stakeholder positions, client sensitivities, business pressures or relationship history. Separate fact from interpretation where needed.
Guardrails: Use only the supplied inputs. Flag missing context rather than filling it in. Do not invent stakeholder positions, client sensitivities, business pressures or relationship history. Separate fact from interpretation where needed.
▶ Output: A practical client engagement prep note covering business context, client POV, stakeholder dynamics, likely questions, Leo's recommended position and the messages or decisions we need to land
B) Growth & portfolio narrative
📌 CoPilot

Current scope and performance notes; known client priorities; any strategic or commercial context relevant to growth; relationship history where relevant.

A clear, commercial story for where we can grow the relationship, grounded in what the client actually needs, with a credible next step rather than a wishlist.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are a commercially minded account lead for Leo UK working on [CLIENT]. Context: We need to identify credible growth opportunities based on the current relationship, scope, performance notes and known client priorities. Task: Draft a growth narrative that shows where we add value today and where we could sensibly grow next. Output: Structure it as 1) Where we add value today, 2) Evidence from the relationship or work, 3) Three credible growth opportunities, 4) Commercial case for each opportunity, 5) What we would need to prove or unlock it, 6) Recommended next move.

Guardrails: Be realistic, avoid wishlist thinking, and flag where the evidence is weak or missing.
Guardrails: Be realistic. Do not invent performance data or overstate the relationship. Flag where evidence is weak or missing.
▶ Output: A growth narrative that shows where Leo adds value today and makes a credible commercial case for where the relationship grows next
3
Client communications
Presentation design, status updates, client emails and reframing tricky messages
▾
This section covers practical client-facing outputs: turning raw content into a clean Leo presentation, turning bullets into a status email, and reframing a message that is difficult to land. AI handles the structure and first draft — you apply judgement, tone, accuracy and knowledge of the relationship.
A) Presentation design
📌 CoPilot — within Microsoft PowerPoint, using the Leo PowerPoint template

Whilst we do most of our presentation design in Keynote, there isn’t currently a practical way to use AI to automate slide design, layout and formatting directly within Keynote. Until that changes, the best workaround is to use PowerPoint and Copilot for the first-pass design work, then bring the finished deck back into Keynote. It’s not a perfect solution, but it’s surprisingly effective and can save a significant amount of time.

Any Keynote presentation can be exported as a PowerPoint file to get started and, once Copilot has redesigned the deck, the resulting PowerPoint file can be opened directly in Keynote for further refinement.

To start: open the Leo PowerPoint template then open CoPilot within PowerPoint. Upload or paste the source document or undesigned presentation into CoPilot and use the starter prompt below. CoPilot will redesign the presentation using the existing template, applying layouts, reducing text density and creating visual hierarchy. Review the output critically. This will not give you a Dave Allen special, but it will give you a clean and tidy first draft to work from: adjust content, correct any inaccuracies and apply your own judgement on what the deck needs to communicate.

A first-draft designed presentation that uses the Leo template's layouts, fonts, colours and visual conventions throughout. This will not give you a Dave Allen special, but it will give you a clean and tidy first draft to work from: adjust content, correct any inaccuracies and apply your own judgement on what the deck needs to communicate.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are a presentation designer and editorial partner for Leo UK. Context: This deck needs to be redesigned inside the active Leo PowerPoint template. The aim is a clean first-draft presentation that keeps the meaning intact, improves structure and makes the story easier to read. Task: Redesign this presentation using only the existing theme, Slide Master layouts, fonts, colours, placeholders and design elements contained within this PowerPoint file. Preserve the meaning, facts, figures, client names, dates and overall narrative logic. Do not remove important content or introduce unsupported claims. For each slide: select the most appropriate existing layout from this presentation; create a clear headline and visual hierarchy; reduce text density by converting long copy into concise bullets, diagrams, timelines, comparison tables or process flows where appropriate; use the existing template's imagery, icons, shapes and visual conventions; keep formatting, spacing and alignment consistent across the deck; prioritise readability and an executive-level presentation style. If a slide contains too much content, split it into additional slides using the existing layouts rather than shrinking the text. Output: Return a redesigned first-draft deck and flag any slides where content was unclear, too dense, duplicated or needed human editorial judgement.

Guardrails: Do not create a new visual identity. Do not use design styles outside this file. Do not change the meaning of the source content. Review the full presentation for consistency when complete.
Guardrails: The output is a first-draft layout only. Check every slide for accuracy, as CoPilot may reorder, condense or reframe content in ways that change meaning. Do not share the output with a client without a thorough human review. The final editorial and design judgement always belongs to a person.
▶ Output: A first-draft designed presentation using the Leo PowerPoint template, with consistent layout, reduced text density and clear visual hierarchy
B) Status email from bullets
📌 CoPilot

A bullet-point summary of where things stand — what is done, what is in progress, what is next, what the client needs to action. Could also be a copy of an internal status report.

A short, direct client email under 150 words that says exactly what is happening and what the client needs to do. No filler.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are the account lead for Leo UK writing to [CLIENT]. Context: We need to turn these bullets into a short client status update that is clear, calm and action-led. Task: Draft a client status email. Output: Structure it as:
1) Subject line
2) One-line TL;DR
3) What is complete
4) What is in progress
5) What happens next
6) What we need from the client
7) Any risks or decisions

Guardrails: Keep it under 150 words. Use a direct, agency voice. Remove corporate filler. Do not invent project detail.
Guardrails: Keep it under 150 words. Use a direct, agency voice. Remove corporate filler. Do not invent project detail.
▶ Output: Short, action-led client status email with a clear ask and no unnecessary words
C) Reframing a tricky message
📌 CoPilot

A brief description of the situation and what happened; the message that needs to land; the desired outcome; any relevant client context or sensitivities.

The hard thing said clearly and professionally. Honest, not defensive, and protecting the relationship while holding our position.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are a senior client lead for Leo UK managing a sensitive message to [CLIENT]. Context: [Briefly explain the situation.] The message we need to land is [INSERT DIFFICULT NEWS OR POSITION]. The desired outcome is [WHAT WE NEED THE CLIENT TO UNDERSTAND OR DO]. Task: Reframe the message so it is honest, clear and relationship-aware. Output:
1) A direct version
2) A softer, relationship-led version
3) A one-line rationale for each
4) Words or phrases to avoid

Guardrails: Do not soften the substance to the point where the message is lost. Keep the tone non-defensive. Flag where the framing needs a senior human call.
Guardrails: Do not soften the substance to the point where the message is lost. Keep the tone non-defensive. Flag where the framing needs a senior human call.
▶ Output: Two versions of the message — direct and relationship-led — with a rationale for each and a note on language to avoid
4
Commercial & scope
Fees, scope docs, commercial rigour and stress-testing
▾
This section focuses on one of the most useful commercial checks AI can support today: stress-testing a fee or scope before it goes to a client. AI can help spot misalignment, surface assumptions and show where the commercial risk sits, but a person always makes the final commercial call.
A) Fee & scope stress-test
📌 CoPilot (Excel) / MRCL where enabled

Fee breakdown; scope doc or brief; any known constraints or client expectations; rate card where relevant.

The maths checks out, assumptions are visible, and it flags where scope and fee don't line up before it reaches the client.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are a commercially minded account lead for Leo UK reviewing work for [CLIENT]. Context: We need to check whether the fee and scope are aligned before this goes to the client. Task: Review the fee breakdown and scope doc and identify where they don't match, where assumptions are unclear and where the risk sits. Output: Structure it as:
1) Summary of the scope as written
2) Assumptions made (explicit and implicit)
3) Issue table with: area / risk / recommended action
4) Commercial decisions required before sign-off
5) Recommended changes

Guardrails: Do not invent scope items or rate assumptions. Flag where data is missing. Any significant commercial decision needs a senior human review before it goes to the client.
Guardrails: Do not invent scope items or rate assumptions. Flag where data is missing. Any significant commercial decision needs a senior human review before it goes to the client.
▶ Output: Structured scope check surfacing misalignments, flagging assumptions and setting out commercial decisions needed before sign-off
B) SOW first draft from a brief
📌 CoPilot / MRCL where enabled

The brief or summary of what has been agreed; standard working assumptions; any exclusions or dependencies already flagged; phasing or milestone context. Previous scoping documents or templates for reference are also helpful.

A solid first draft that follows a clear structure, with deliverables, phases, assumptions and exclusions set out. A person then sharpens it. Never treat it as final without human review.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are an experienced account lead for Leo UK drafting a review-ready SOW for [CLIENT]. Context: We have a brief and need a structured first draft that follows our standard working style. Task: Draft a first-cut Statement of Work from the brief. Output: Structure it as:
1) Background and objective
2) Scope of deliverables
3) Phasing and key milestones
4) Roles and responsibilities
5) Assumptions
6) Out of scope / exclusions
7) Dependencies and client inputs
8) Commercial decisions required
9) Open questions

Guardrails: Do not write final legal wording. Flag anything that needs human or legal review. Treat the output as a working draft, not a final document.
Guardrails: Do not write final legal wording. Flag anything that needs human or legal review. Treat the output as a working draft, not a final document.
▶ Output: Review-ready SOW first draft with deliverables, phasing, assumptions and open questions clearly set out
5
Cultural & competitive context
Competitor landscape, market context and cultural framing for briefs and client conversations
▾
At Leo, understanding the competitive landscape and understanding what's alive in culture aren't two separate exercises — they're the same question asked from different angles. Populist Creativity is about finding the territory where people are already having conversations; that means knowing what competitors are doing AND what broader cultural currents are shaping the category. This is one workflow that produces one integrated output.
Cultural & competitive context pack
📌 CoPilot / MRCL where enabled

Client brief or current strategic question; known competitor set; category and audience context; any existing research or planning notes; relevant time period for the scan.

A grounded, integrated view of the competitive landscape and the cultural conversations shaping it, with a clear 'so what' for the brief or client conversation. Sourced, not speculative, and written so an account lead can use it to articulate cultural relevance to a client with confidence.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are a strategy-informed account lead for Leo UK working on [CLIENT] in [CATEGORY]. Context: We need an integrated view of the competitive landscape and the cultural conversations shaping it — not as separate outputs, but as one connected picture that makes the brief or client conversation sharper. Task: Build a cultural and competitive context pack from the supplied materials and any connected data sources available. Output: Structure it as follows:

1. CATEGORY SNAPSHOT: What is the current state of the category? What has shifted recently and why does it matter?

2. COMPETITOR MOVES: A table covering the top 3–4 competitors with columns for: competitor / recent activity / positioning / why it matters for our client.

3. WHAT PEOPLE ARE TALKING ABOUT: What conversations, behaviours or cultural moments are shaping this category right now, outside of advertising? What are people sharing, arguing over or reacting to? Please review social channels, Reddit, editorial and anywhere that real human conversations take place.

4. POSITIONING THEMES: What are the recurring themes across the competitive set? Where is the space that is unclaimed or underleveraged?

5. OPPORTUNITIES & RISKS: What does this mean for our client's brief or positioning? What should they lean into? What should they avoid?

6. THE SO WHAT: One clear paragraph that connects the competitive picture and the cultural context into a single strategic observation the team can brief from.

7. SOURCE TABLE: Source / date / key point, for everything cited.

Guardrails: Cite everything. Separate confirmed fact from interpretation throughout. Do not invent competitor claims or cultural references — flag where information needs checking or is based on inference.
Guardrails: Cite everything. Separate confirmed fact from interpretation. Do not invent competitor claims or cultural references — flag where information needs checking or is based on inference.
▶ Output: Integrated context pack covering competitive landscape and cultural conversations shaping the category, with a clear strategic 'so what'
6
Creative development & review
Brief review and clarification before strategy starts; first-pass risk review of creative ideas; image and video reference to support idea development and the client sell
▾
This section covers four connected uses across creative development: clarifying a client brief before strategy starts, getting an early risk read on a creative concept before it goes to a client, and using image and video generation tools to help bring ideas to life in the presentation.
A) Brief review & clarification
📌 CoPilot

Client brief and any wider brand or business context.

A messy or incomplete client brief turned into something clear enough for the agency to act on. The first pass asks: is the brief clear? The second asks: what needs tightening before we can develop the overarching strategy and creative brief?

Starter prompt 
Role: You are a strategically minded account lead for Leo UK reviewing a client brief for [CLIENT / PROJECT NAME]. Context: Work only from the supplied client brief, brand context, existing notes, mandatories and constraints. Task: Simplify, check and improve the brief so the agency has a clearer starting point for strategy. Output: Structure your answer under the headings below.

STEP 1: MAKE IT CLEAR

1. WHAT THE CLIENT IS REALLY ASKING: Cut through the background to the core request. What does the client need the agency to solve or deliver?

2. BUSINESS OBJECTIVE: Is the commercial or business objective clear? Rewrite it in plain English. If it is missing or vague, say what needs clarifying.

3. COMMUNICATION OBJECTIVE: What does the work need people to think, feel or do? Rewrite this clearly. If it is missing or generic, say what needs clarifying.

4. MANDATORIES & CONSTRAINTS: Pull out all known mandatories, budget, timings, deliverables, approval stages, key stakeholders, legal or brand restrictions, dependencies and watchouts.

5. THE SIMPLE VERSION: Rewrite the brief in one short paragraph, no jargon, so the internal team can understand it quickly.

STEP 2: MAKE IT BETTER

6. IS IT READY FOR STRATEGY? Be honest. What is clear, what is missing, what is contradictory, and what would slow the strategy team down?

7. QUESTIONS BACK TO CLIENT: List the questions the account team should ask before the brief moves on, grouped by objective, audience, mandatories, timing, budget and approvals.

8. STRATEGIC STARTING POINT: Turn the clarified brief into a useful agency starting point for strategists. Keep it practical, not over-written.

9. CLARIFIED AGENCY BRIEF: Rewrite the brief as a sharper internal agency brief that strategy can use to develop the overarching strategy and creative brief.

Guardrails: Only use the supplied brief and context. Flag missing objectives, audience information, budget, timings, stakeholders, mandatories and approval requirements. Challenge the brief rather than simply tidying it. Do not invent brand knowledge, category facts, commercial assumptions or client sensitivities.
Guardrails: Only use the supplied brief and context. Flag missing objectives, audience information, budget, timings, stakeholders, mandatories and approval requirements. Challenge the brief rather than simply tidying it. Do not invent brand knowledge, category facts, commercial assumptions or client sensitivities.
▶ Output: Clarified client brief, list of questions back to the client, and a sharper internal agency brief for strategy to build from
B) Concept review
📌 CoPilot concept review agent

The creative idea, concept or territory; brief; brand and client context; category; any known mandatories, restrictions or compliance requirements.

A fast, structured first-pass view across competitive, compliance, IP, claims, brand, channel and sector risks — surfaced early enough to shape further development, not raised for the first time in a client meeting.

🔗

Open the CoPilot concept review agent directly and share the creative idea or territory along with the relevant brief and client context. The agent will give you a structured first-pass view across the key risk areas: competitive, compliance, IP, claims, brand, channel and sector.

Guardrails: The output is a first pass to guide further development, not a replacement for legal or compliance advice. If the agent flags a significant risk, escalate it through the proper channel — do not rely on the AI output alone to clear an issue.
▶ Output: First-pass risk view across key risk areas, with issues flagged clearly enough to guide further development or escalation
C) Image reference & visual mood
🖼 Google Nano Banana / Imagen

Creative territory or idea; mood references; any brand visual world context; audience notes; any restrictions on logos, likenesses, locations or IP.

Fast, on-territory visual reference that helps bring a strategic idea or creative concept to life in a client presentation — showing intent and direction without implying a finished asset. Reference only; never presented as final creative.

Starter prompt 
Role: You are an account lead creating visual reference to support a client presentation. Context: Work only from the supplied brand, audience and creative territory context for [CLIENT / PROJECT NAME]. Task: Create image-reference directions that bring the idea or strategic territory to life visually. Output: Produce 3 to 4 distinct visual directions.

Territory / idea: [DESCRIBE IN 1–2 SENTENCES]
Generate visual reference that shows: [mood / lighting / colour world / era / composition].
Style direction: [e.g. cinematic, documentary, editorial, graphic, surreal].
Produce 3–4 distinct visual directions so we can see range, not one answer.

Guardrails: Do not use real brand logos, real people's likenesses, third-party IP, or anything that implies a final asset.
Guardrails: Reference only. Avoid real brand logos, real people's likenesses and third-party IP.
▶ Output: 3–4 on-territory visual mood directions to support idea development or a client presentation
D) Motion & video reference
🎬 Google VEO

Territory or idea; mood and pace references; visual style notes; brand restrictions; anything that must not appear in the motion reference.

Short motion reference that communicates feel, pace and tone — enough to help a client understand the energy of an idea before it goes into production. Reference only; never presented as finished creative.

Starter prompt 
Territory / idea: [DESCRIBE IN 1–2 SENTENCES]
Generate a short motion reference (4–6 seconds) that captures: [mood / pace / tone].
Style direction: [e.g. documentary, cinematic, social-native, graphic].
Keep it short and simple — just enough to feel the idea move.

Guardrails: Reference only. Keep it short and simple. Avoid real brand assets, real people's likenesses and third-party IP.
Guardrails: Reference only. Keep it short and simple. Avoid real brand assets, real people's likenesses and third-party IP.

Guardrails

Legal & safe use

These apply to every use case, every time. They are non-negotiable and consistent across all Leo UK departmental playbooks.

🔒

Client data & consent

No client data goes into any tool until the account's legal position is confirmed. MRCL client use follows the Account Lead → Legal Partner process: notice, consent, or new AI terms as advised. Keep a record of all client communications.

🏢

Stay in approved environments

Agency and client workspaces only. No personal accounts, and no public LLMs for client work. Each client's work stays within that client's environment.

👤

Human owns the output

AI drafts, a person decides. Nothing client-facing goes out without a human check for accuracy, tone and nuance.

🗂

Keep work contained

Work done on one client stays within that client's environment. MRCL is sandboxed within Publicis and nothing you input trains public models.

⚠

Concept review is a first pass, not a legal sign-off

The concept review agent gives a structured early view of potential risks. It is not a replacement for legal or compliance advice. If it flags something significant, escalate it through the proper channel — do not rely on the AI output alone to clear an issue.

❓

If in doubt

Check with your client lead before using AI on anything client-facing or commercially sensitive.

The client legal process in one line

Account Lead contacts their Legal Partner → Legal confirms the category (no action / notice / consent / new AI terms) → agree the approach → get client buy-in and record it → Legal maintains the central tracker.

Prompt writing cheat sheet

Write prompts that actually work

Good prompts are not magic words. They are clear instructions. At Leo, a good prompt should get you somewhere commercially and culturally useful — not just structurally correct.

The basic structure

Role

Tell AI who to be

Account lead, Managing Partner, operations lead, strategy-informed account lead. Give it a perspective it can work from.

Context

Explain the situation

Client, agency, situation, audience, level of sensitivity and why the output is needed.

Task

Be explicit about the job

Draft, summarise, compare, stress-test, reframe, turn notes into actions. One clear verb.

Output

Define the exact shape

Email, one-pager, table, deck outline, action log, decision note, checklist.

Guardrails

Say what not to do

Do not guess. Do not overclaim. Flag assumptions. Use only supplied inputs. Mark anything unclear as TBC.

Reusable prompt frame

Copy and adapt this

"Role: Act as a [role] for Leo UK working on [client/brand]. Context: We need to [explain the situation and audience]. Task: Your job is to [specific task]. Inputs: Use [emails / notes / deck / data / brief] only. Output: Return [format] structured as [headings, table columns or slide sections]. Guardrails: Do not guess, do not invent missing detail, flag assumptions, and mark anything unclear as TBC."

Make it better by adding

🎯 Audience

Client, internal team, leadership, Finance, Legal, creative review. Who's reading changes everything.

🗣 Tone

Clear, direct, warm, firm, commercial, neutral, action-led. Name it explicitly.

📏 Length

One paragraph, 150 words, one page, five bullets, ten-slide outline. Constrain it.

💬 The cultural question

When building context or shaping a brief, ask the AI what people are already talking about in this space — and how that should shape the work or the sell.

Before you use the output

Quality check

  • Check facts, dates, names, numbers and client references.
  • Remove anything that sounds generic, inflated or unlike Leo.
  • Make the judgement call yourself. AI can shape the work, but it cannot own the decision.
  • Do not use client data unless the account's legal position and approved environment are confirmed.
